5G networks introduce the concept of network slicing,
allowing multiple logical slices to share a common physical
infrastructure while supporting services with diverse and often
conflicting performance requirements [1], [2]. Applications
such as enhanced Mobile Broadband (eMBB), Ultra Reli-
able Low Latency Communications (URLLC), and massive
Machine Type Communications (mMTC) operate in funda-
mentally different regimes. eMBB prioritizes high data rates,
URLLC requires stringent latency and reliability guarantees,
and mMTC focuses on scalable connectivity for large numbers
of low rate devices. These heterogeneous requirements place
continuous pressure on the underlying infrastructure to allocate
resources in a timely, efficient, and Service Level Agreement
(SLA) compliant manner.
In practice, slice performance depends on multiple resource
domains. Compute capacity at user plane and edge functions
determines packet processing latency, radio access network
bandwidth limits the volume of traffic reaching the core,
and transport and backhaul capacity directly affect end-to-
end delay. A bottleneck in any of these domains can lead to
noticeable performance degradation. Insufficient CPU capacity
increases processing delay, limited radio resources constrain
achievable throughput, and congestion in transport links in-
creases latency [3].
Because slice demand in 5G networks can change rapidly
due to user mobility and bursty application behavior, static or
infrequently updated resource allocations are often inadequate.
Even modest under-provisioning of compute or radio resources
can result in significant latency increases for delay sensi-
tive slices, as observed in prior work [3]. These challenges
motivate the need for slice controllers that operate at fine
time granularity and react to real-time conditions. In this
work, we focus on a single eMBB style slice with a 1 s
control period. However, the proposed RL-Loop framework is
designed to extend to multiple slices by applying the control
policy independently using slice specific key performance
indicators and normalized inputs.
A significant body of existing work on slice resource
management relies on static provisioning, where allocations
are chosen based on peak demand and remain fixed throughout
operation. This approach simplifies deployment but wastes

For each run, we select a CPU limit and a bandwidth setting
for the slice and keep them fixed while the traffic evolves. At
each one-second interval, the system logs four values: the CPU
usage of the user-plane function (in millicores), the throughput
observed at the UE side (computed from packet captures using
tshark), the CPU allocation chosen by the RL agent, and
the corresponding reward value returned by the environment.
These logs are stored as CSV and text files and are used
both to train the agent offline and to compute aggregate metrics
such as average CPU allocation and qualitative QoS trends.
MicroOpt is a model-driven optimization framework that
was introduced in prior work [7]. It learns a differentiable
performance model that maps traffic load and resource levels
to a predicted QoS value. An optimizer then uses this model to
select resource allocations that satisfy a QoS target while keep-
ing resource usage low. In its original evaluation, MicroOpt
uses traffic profiles derived from the Telecom Italia dataset
and runs in a simulation environment.
In this paper, we do not reimplement or execute MicroOpt
on our testbed. Instead, we use the published MicroOpt results
as an indicative baseline. In particular, we rely on the reported

5G performance in a smart-factory environment and reported
substantial improvements in throughput and latency compared
to LTE, highlighting the benefits of adaptive, slice-aware
control for industrial workloads. Xing et al. [10] examined
dynamic baseband and radio resource allocation for eMBB
slices in heterogeneous cloud radio access network (H-CRAN)
architectures and observed improvements in both throughput
and QoS under varying load conditions. These works confirm
the value of adaptive control, although many focus on a single
resource type or rely on simplified test environments.
Despite recent progress, the practical adoption of AI-driven
slice control still faces several challenges. Scalability and
cross-domain coordination remain difficult when slices span
heterogeneous RAN and core environments. Recent surveys
on network slicing orchestration [17] note that current man-
agement frameworks struggle with slice lifecycle automation,
performance isolation, and the integration of AI/ML compo-
nents into existing network function virtualization (NFV) /
software-defined networking (SDN) architectures.
Security and reliability concerns also persist. As networks
move toward zero-touch automation, AI-based controllers be-
come part of the attack surface. Batewela et al. [18] highlight
that orchestration functions introduce new vulnerabilities re-
lated to real-time monitoring, intent translation, and policy
enforcement. Ensuring stable and explainable behavior from
learning-based controllers remains an open problem, particu-
larly under non-stationary traffic or adversarial conditions.
Existing work explores both model-driven and RL-based
methods, but most solutions treat these directions separately
and rarely evaluate them in a full end-to-end 5G testbed. In
this paper, we introduce RL-Loop, a closed-loop controller
that uses real-time feedback to adjust CPU allocation for slice
functions. MicroOpt is used only offline to provide an initial
reference point, while all online decisions are made by the
RL agent operating directly on network measurements. This
combination addresses limitations in prior static, reactive, and
prediction-only methods and provides a practical framework
for adaptive slice control.

A. Experiment Setup
We evaluate RL-Loop on the end-to-end 5G testbed de-
scribed in Section III, built with Open5GS for the core network
and UERANSIM for the radio access network (RAN) and user
equipment (UE) emulation [21]. All core functions, the gNB,
and UE instances run as virtual machines on a Hyper-V host
with an Intel Xeon Gold 6348 CPU and 512 GB of RAM.
Each VM runs Ubuntu 24.04 LTS in a private network.
Traffic is generated by emulated UEs streaming a 4K
YouTube video [22]. User arrivals follow a truncated normal
distribution with a mean between 1 and 5 users/second,
using statistics inspired by the Telecom Italia trace [19]. This
produces realistic but controllable variations in offered load.
During each run, the RL agent interacts with the testbed for
900 seconds. At every one second control interval it receives
the current traffic and CPU usage, selects a normalized CPU
allocation, and the environment applies the corresponding
CPU limit (in millicores) to the user plane process using
Linux cgroup controls. We record four quantities at one-
second resolution: CPU usage of the user-plane function (in
millicores), UE-side throughput extracted from packet captures
usingtshark, the CPU allocation selected by the RL agent,
and the reward returned by the environment.
All logs are stored as CSV or text files and are used to
compute the mean CPU allocation over the run and to study
how throughput and reward evolve over time.

Existing closed-loop service assurance mechanisms often react to performance degradations, leading to potential Service Level Agreements (SLAs) violations and inefficient resource utilization, as highlighted in recent studies [1, 2].
To meet the evolving requirements of both network operators and end-users, these challenges must be effectively addressed.
In particular, B5G networks will demand greater load adaptability and scalability to support the rapid growth of 5G and B5G applications. Furthermore, network efficiency can be increased by mitigating congestion and service disruptions.

5G networks introduce the concept of network slicing,
allowing multiple logical slices to share a common physical
infrastructure while supporting services with diverse and often
conflicting performance requirements [1], [2]. Applications
such as enhanced Mobile Broadband (eMBB), Ultra Reli-
able Low Latency Communications (URLLC), and massive
Machine Type Communications (mMTC) operate in funda-
mentally different regimes. eMBB prioritizes high data rates,
URLLC requires stringent latency and reliability guarantees,
and mMTC focuses on scalable connectivity for large numbers
of low rate devices. These heterogeneous requirements place
continuous pressure on the underlying infrastructure to allocate
resources in a timely, efficient, and Service Level Agreement
(SLA) compliant manner.
In practice, slice performance depends on multiple resource
domains. Compute capacity at user plane and edge functions
determines packet processing latency, radio access network
bandwidth limits the volume of traffic reaching the core,
and transport and backhaul capacity directly affect end-to-
end delay. A bottleneck in any of these domains can lead to
noticeable performance degradation. Insufficient CPU capacity
increases processing delay, limited radio resources constrain
achievable throughput, and congestion in transport links in-
creases latency [3].
Because slice demand in 5G networks can change rapidly
due to user mobility and bursty application behavior, static or
infrequently updated resource allocations are often inadequate.
Even modest under-provisioning of compute or radio resources
can result in significant latency increases for delay sensi-
tive slices, as observed in prior work [3]. These challenges
motivate the need for slice controllers that operate at fine
time granularity and react to real-time conditions. In this
work, we focus on a single eMBB style slice with a 1 s
control period. However, the proposed RL-Loop framework is
designed to extend to multiple slices by applying the control
policy independently using slice specific key performance
indicators and normalized inputs.
A significant body of existing work on slice resource
management relies on static provisioning, where allocations
are chosen based on peak demand and remain fixed throughout
operation. This approach simplifies deployment but wastes

For each run, we select a CPU limit and a bandwidth setting
for the slice and keep them fixed while the traffic evolves. At
each one-second interval, the system logs four values: the CPU
usage of the user-plane function (in millicores), the throughput
observed at the UE side (computed from packet captures using
tshark), the CPU allocation chosen by the RL agent, and
the corresponding reward value returned by the environment.
These logs are stored as CSV and text files and are used
both to train the agent offline and to compute aggregate metrics
such as average CPU allocation and qualitative QoS trends.
MicroOpt is a model-driven optimization framework that
was introduced in prior work [7]. It learns a differentiable
performance model that maps traffic load and resource levels
to a predicted QoS value. An optimizer then uses this model to
select resource allocations that satisfy a QoS target while keep-
ing resource usage low. In its original evaluation, MicroOpt
uses traffic profiles derived from the Telecom Italia dataset
and runs in a simulation environment.
In this paper, we do not reimplement or execute MicroOpt
on our testbed. Instead, we use the published MicroOpt results
as an indicative baseline. In particular, we rely on the reported
3

5G performance in a smart-factory environment and reported
substantial improvements in throughput and latency compared
to LTE, highlighting the benefits of adaptive, slice-aware
control for industrial workloads. Xing et al. [10] examined
dynamic baseband and radio resource allocation for eMBB
slices in heterogeneous cloud radio access network (H-CRAN)
architectures and observed improvements in both throughput
and QoS under varying load conditions. These works confirm
the value of adaptive control, although many focus on a single
resource type or rely on simplified test environments.
Despite recent progress, the practical adoption of AI-driven
slice control still faces several challenges. Scalability and
cross-domain coordination remain difficult when slices span
heterogeneous RAN and core environments. Recent surveys
on network slicing orchestration [17] note that current man-
agement frameworks struggle with slice lifecycle automation,
performance isolation, and the integration of AI/ML compo-
nents into existing network function virtualization (NFV) /
software-defined networking (SDN) architectures.
Security and reliability concerns also persist. As networks
move toward zero-touch automation, AI-based controllers be-
come part of the attack surface. Batewela et al. [18] highlight
that orchestration functions introduce new vulnerabilities re-
lated to real-time monitoring, intent translation, and policy
enforcement. Ensuring stable and explainable behavior from
learning-based controllers remains an open problem, particu-
larly under non-stationary traffic or adversarial conditions.
Existing work explores both model-driven and RL-based
methods, but most solutions treat these directions separately
and rarely evaluate them in a full end-to-end 5G testbed. In
this paper, we introduce RL-Loop, a closed-loop controller
that uses real-time feedback to adjust CPU allocation for slice
functions. MicroOpt is used only offline to provide an initial
reference point, while all online decisions are made by the
RL agent operating directly on network measurements. This
combination addresses limitations in prior static, reactive, and
prediction-only methods and provides a practical framework
for adaptive slice control.

5G networks introduce the concept of network slicing,
allowing multiple logical slices to share a common physical
infrastructure while supporting services with diverse and often
conflicting performance requirements [1], [2]. Applications
such as enhanced Mobile Broadband (eMBB), Ultra Reli-
able Low Latency Communications (URLLC), and massive
Machine Type Communications (mMTC) operate in funda-
mentally different regimes. eMBB prioritizes high data rates,
URLLC requires stringent latency and reliability guarantees,
and mMTC focuses on scalable connectivity for large numbers
of low rate devices. These heterogeneous requirements place
continuous pressure on the underlying infrastructure to allocate
resources in a timely, efficient, and Service Level Agreement
(SLA) compliant manner.
In practice, slice performance depends on multiple resource
domains. Compute capacity at user plane and edge functions
determines packet processing latency, radio access network
bandwidth limits the volume of traffic reaching the core,
and transport and backhaul capacity directly affect end-to-
end delay. A bottleneck in any of these domains can lead to
noticeable performance degradation. Insufficient CPU capacity
increases processing delay, limited radio resources constrain
achievable throughput, and congestion in transport links in-
creases latency [3].
Because slice demand in 5G networks can change rapidly
due to user mobility and bursty application behavior, static or
infrequently updated resource allocations are often inadequate.
Even modest under-provisioning of compute or radio resources
can result in significant latency increases for delay sensi-
tive slices, as observed in prior work [3]. These challenges
motivate the need for slice controllers that operate at fine
time granularity and react to real-time conditions. In this
work, we focus on a single eMBB style slice with a 1 s
control period. However, the proposed RL-Loop framework is
designed to extend to multiple slices by applying the control
policy independently using slice specific key performance
indicators and normalized inputs.
A significant body of existing work on slice resource

are chosen based on peak demand and remain fixed throughout

performance model that maps traffic load and resource levels
to a predicted QoS value. An optimizer then uses this model to
select resource allocations that satisfy a QoS target while keep-

cross-domain coordination remain difficult when slices span

proposed_tests: The event-driven asynchronous system will demonstrate at least a 30% reduction in P99 control latency during spikes compared to a synchronous hierarchical baseline.
The event-driven asynchronous system will demonstrate at least a 20% reduction in communication overhead compared to the synchronous baseline.

strengths: Clearly distinguishes between fast local control (sub-second) and slow global coordination (seconds), addressing latency bottlenecks.
Provides specific, quantifiable rejection criteria (30% latency reduction, 20% overhead reduction) which enhances scientific rigor.
Leverages PPO for local agents, a technique proven feasible in 5G slice control contexts as evidenced by the RL-Loop source.
Addresses the scalability and communication overhead issues inherent in synchronous hierarchical or federated approaches.
weaknesses: The assumption that local PPO agents can independently maintain SLA compliance during severe spikes without immediate global intervention is optimistic and may lead to transient SLA violations before the 5-10s global reconciliation loop activates.
The definition of 'spike events' (e.g., 80% buffer occupancy) is heuristic and may not generalize across different slice types (uRLLC vs eMBB) without significant tuning.

The comparison baseline (synchronous polling every 1 second) is somewhat weak; modern distributed systems often use event-driven mechanisms even in hierarchical structures, so the novelty of 'asynchronous' vs 'synchronous' might be overstated if the baseline is not state-of-the-art.

review_comments: The hypothesis is strong, well-defined, and directly addresses the research goal. It improves upon previous ambiguities by specifying the asynchronous, event-driven nature of the global coordination layer. The feasibility is high given the existence of 5G testbeds and PPO implementations for slice control. The main risk lies in the assumption that local autonomy can fully protect SLAs during the 5-10 second window before global reconciliation, which is a critical experimental variable. The provided sources support the feasibility of RL-based control and the limitations of static/synchronous methods, though they do not explicitly validate the specific 'asynchronous reconciliation' architecture proposed here.
selected_hypothesis.text:
Hypothesis: A closed-loop multi-agent framework that decouples real-time local bandwidth adjustments from global coordination using an event-driven, asynchronous reconciliation mechanism will maintain SLA compliance during traffic spikes with lower end-to-end control latency and reduced communication overhead compared to synchronous hierarchical aggregation.

Rationale: The parent hypothesis (G2034) identified a valid hierarchical structure but suffered from ambiguity regarding the upper-tier coordination mechanism and the specific dynamics of bandwidth versus CPU allocation. This hypothesis repairs these weaknesses by specifying an 'Event-Driven Asynchronous' architecture. Instead of periodic polling or synchronous model averaging (which causes latency and overhead in FedMARL-style systems), lower-tier slice agents operate independently with local PPO policies for immediate, sub-second bandwidth reallocation within a pre-allocated local budget. Communication to the upper-tier aggregator is triggered only by 'spike events' (e.g., local buffer occupancy exceeding 80% or QoS degradation metrics crossing thresholds). The upper-tier agent does not send immediate control commands but instead issues 'Budget Reconciliation Messages' (BRMs) asynchronously to adjust the global bandwidth envelope for the affected slice over a slower, non-critical timescale (e.g., 5-10 seconds). This preserves the novelty of hierarchical multi-agent control while making the mechanism specific and implementable: it separates the fast, reactive local loop from the slow, strategic global loop, ensuring that real-time latency guarantees are met by local autonomy, while global efficiency is handled by asynchronous negotiation.

Feasibility: Implement a two-tier simulation/testbed environment. 1) Define local PPO agents for 3-5 5G slices (uRLLC, eMBB, mMTC) with state spaces including current bandwidth allocation, queue depth, and packet loss rate. 2) Define an upper-tier aggregator that listens for asynchronous spike events (messages containing slice ID, current load, and requested budget delta) and responds with BRMs containing new minimum/maximum bandwidth bounds. 3) Simulate traffic spikes (sudden 200% increase in eMBB demand) and measure: (a) P99 latency for bandwidth adjustment (should be <100ms for local actions), (b) total inter-agent message volume during spikes, and (c) SLA violation rate. 4) Compare against a synchronous hierarchical baseline where the upper tier polls all agents every 1 second and issues immediate constraints. Rejection criterion: If the event-driven asynchronous system does not demonstrate at least a 30% reduction in P99 control latency during spikes or a 20% reduction in communication overhead compared to the synchronous baseline, while maintaining comparable SLA compliance, the hypothesis is rejected.

5G networks introduce the concept of network slicing,
allowing multiple logical slices to share a common physical
infrastructure while supporting services with diverse and often
conflicting performance requirements [1], [2]. Applications
such as enhanced Mobile Broadband (eMBB), Ultra Reli-
able Low Latency Communications (URLLC), and massive
Machine Type Communications (mMTC) operate in funda-
mentally different regimes. eMBB prioritizes high data rates,
URLLC requires stringent latency and reliability guarantees,
and mMTC focuses on scalable connectivity for large numbers
of low rate devices. These heterogeneous requirements place
continuous pressure on the underlying infrastructure to allocate
resources in a timely, efficient, and Service Level Agreement
(SLA) compliant manner.
In practice, slice performance depends on multiple resource
domains. Compute capacity at user plane and edge functions
determines packet processing latency, radio access network
bandwidth limits the volume of traffic reaching the core,
and transport and backhaul capacity directly affect end-to-
end delay. A bottleneck in any of these domains can lead to
noticeable performance degradation. Insufficient CPU capacity
increases processing delay, limited radio resources constrain
achievable throughput, and congestion in transport links in-
creases latency [3].
Because slice demand in 5G networks can change rapidly
due to user mobility and bursty application behavior, static or
infrequently updated resource allocations are often inadequate.
Even modest under-provisioning of compute or radio resources
can result in significant latency increases for delay sensi-
tive slices, as observed in prior work [3]. These challenges
motivate the need for slice controllers that operate at fine
time granularity and react to real-time conditions. In this
work, we focus on a single eMBB style slice with a 1 s
control period. However, the proposed RL-Loop framework is
designed to extend to multiple slices by applying the control
policy independently using slice specific key performance
indicators and normalized inputs.
A significant body of existing work on slice resource
management relies on static provisioning, where allocations
are chosen based on peak demand and remain fixed throughout
operation. This approach simplifies deployment but wastes

For each run, we select a CPU limit and a bandwidth setting
for the slice and keep them fixed while the traffic evolves. At
each one-second interval, the system logs four values: the CPU
usage of the user-plane function (in millicores), the throughput
observed at the UE side (computed from packet captures using

These logs are stored as CSV and text files and are used

such as average CPU allocation and qualitative QoS trends.
MicroOpt is a model-driven optimization framework that
was introduced in prior work [7]. It learns a differentiable
performance model that maps traffic load and resource levels
to a predicted QoS value. An optimizer then uses this model to
select resource allocations that satisfy a QoS target while keep-
ing resource usage low. In its original evaluation, MicroOpt
uses traffic profiles derived from the Telecom Italia dataset
and runs in a simulation environment.
In this paper, we do not reimplement or execute MicroOpt
on our testbed. Instead, we use the published MicroOpt results
as an indicative baseline. In particular, we rely on the reported

5G performance in a smart-factory environment and reported
substantial improvements in throughput and latency compared
to LTE, highlighting the benefits of adaptive, slice-aware
control for industrial workloads. Xing et al. [10] examined
dynamic baseband and radio resource allocation for eMBB
slices in heterogeneous cloud radio access network (H-CRAN)
architectures and observed improvements in both throughput
and QoS under varying load conditions. These works confirm
the value of adaptive control, although many focus on a single
resource type or rely on simplified test environments.
Despite recent progress, the practical adoption of AI-driven
slice control still faces several challenges. Scalability and
cross-domain coordination remain difficult when slices span
heterogeneous RAN and core environments. Recent surveys
on network slicing orchestration [17] note that current man-
agement frameworks struggle with slice lifecycle automation,
performance isolation, and the integration of AI/ML compo-
nents into existing network function virtualization (NFV) /
software-defined networking (SDN) architectures.
Security and reliability concerns also persist. As networks
move toward zero-touch automation, AI-based controllers be-
come part of the attack surface. Batewela et al. [18] highlight
that orchestration functions introduce new vulnerabilities re-
lated to real-time monitoring, intent translation, and policy
enforcement. Ensuring stable and explainable behavior from
learning-based controllers remains an open problem, particu-
larly under non-stationary traffic or adversarial conditions.
Existing work explores both model-driven and RL-based
methods, but most solutions treat these directions separately
and rarely evaluate them in a full end-to-end 5G testbed. In
this paper, we introduce RL-Loop, a closed-loop controller
that uses real-time feedback to adjust CPU allocation for slice
functions. MicroOpt is used only offline to provide an initial
reference point, while all online decisions are made by the
RL agent operating directly on network measurements. This
combination addresses limitations in prior static, reactive, and
prediction-only methods and provides a practical framework
for adaptive slice control.

A. Experiment Setup
We evaluate RL-Loop on the end-to-end 5G testbed de-
scribed in Section III, built with Open5GS for the core network
and UERANSIM for the radio access network (RAN) and user
equipment (UE) emulation [21]. All core functions, the gNB,
and UE instances run as virtual machines on a Hyper-V host
with an Intel Xeon Gold 6348 CPU and 512 GB of RAM.
Each VM runs Ubuntu 24.04 LTS in a private network.
Traffic is generated by emulated UEs streaming a 4K
YouTube video [22]. User arrivals follow a truncated normal
distribution with a mean between 1 and 5 users/second,
using statistics inspired by the Telecom Italia trace [19]. This
produces realistic but controllable variations in offered load.
During each run, the RL agent interacts with the testbed for
900 seconds. At every one second control interval it receives
the current traffic and CPU usage, selects a normalized CPU
allocation, and the environment applies the corresponding
CPU limit (in millicores) to the user plane process using
Linux cgroup controls. We record four quantities at one-
second resolution: CPU usage of the user-plane function (in
millicores), UE-side throughput extracted from packet captures
usingtshark, the CPU allocation selected by the RL agent,
and the reward returned by the environment.
All logs are stored as CSV or text files and are used to
compute the mean CPU allocation over the run and to study
how throughput and reward evolve over time.
